lessons.title: 1.1 Basic Shading Techniques
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Shading transforms the simple shape of an object into a proper form and creates depth on a flat surface.
  • Pencil tip techniques (Figure 1.1): flat sketch, round sharpened to flat tip, tip of sharp point, side of round and blunt round.
  • Soft pencil marks: 2B scribbles, 3B herringbone and smudged tone, 4B pushed zigzag, 5B irregular dots, 6B rubbed graphite layers.
  • Graphite pencils range from 8B (softest, darkest) to 6H (hardest, lightest); HB is the middle grade.
  • Graphite is a form of carbon; the pencil 'lead' is graphite compressed and baked to varying degrees of hardness.

Q: What is shading? Describe the basic shading techniques and the use of the pencil tip.

Shading helps to transform the simple shape of any object into a proper form of the object. It helps to create a kind of depth to a flat surface. The basic techniques for pencil strokes should be observed and practiced to achieve different shades with pencils. Experimenting with these strokes students will learn the control over pencil and its strokes. Different techniques of using the pencil tip (Figure 1.1) are: Flat sketch, Round sharpened to flat tip, Tip of sharp point, Side of round and Blunt round. Soft pencil marks (Figure 1.2) include: 2B - Horizontal rows of scribbled shading; Scribbled lines implying a knitted texture and shadow; Vertical scribble, creating a soft texture and shading; 3B - Heavy herringbone texture; Smudged tone (with the finger) to create atmosphere; Random marks marking implying a rough texture; 4B - A pushed zigzag line using the side of the pencil; Rows of vertical scribble, progressing from dark to light; Regular dashes of tone; 5B - Irregular dots, creating an implied texture, perhaps a gravel path; Wooly scribble creating a textured surface; Open zigzag lines create tone and texture; 6B - Layer of graphite rubbed diagonally to create atmospheres; Vertical lines rubbed horizontally and then vertical lines drawn over the top to create a woven texture; Tone rubbed vertically and then horizontally to create a woven texture.

Q: What do the different numbers of graphite pencils (8B to 6H) show?

Figure 1.3 shows the tones of different numbers of pencils. Graphite wooden pencils range from 8B, 7B, 6B, 5B, 4B, 3B, 2B, B, HB, F, H, 2H, 3H, 4H, 5H to 6H. The B pencils are soft and give dark tones (8B is the softest and darkest), while the H pencils are hard and give light tones (6H is the hardest and lightest). HB is the middle grade. A form of carbon which leaves a shiny metallic gray color on a surface when moved across it is graphite; the most common form of graphite is the "lead" inside a pencil, compressed and baked to varying degrees of hardness.

lessons.title: 1.3 Making of a Portrait Drawing
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A portrait can be depicted from different directions: front side portrait, side profile portrait and three quarter portrait.
  • The basic shape of the head is like a ball flattened on the sides; the large ball-like circle is the cranial mass, and the nose, lips and chin lie outside this circle.
  • Front view proportions: the eyes lie on the central horizontal line; halving the chin-to-eyes portion gives the end of the nose; halving the nose-to-chin portion gives the ending point of the lips.
  • The hairline is one third down from the top of the head to the eyes portion; the eyebrows are on the line just above the ears.
  • Labelled lines of the diagram: vertical centerline, hairline, brow line, horizontal centerline, nose, bottom lip and chin.

Q: Portrait Practice #1: What are the basic guidelines for learning the basic shape of the head?

Students will learn the normal proportion of a face using the basic guidelines for understanding the basic structure and making a proportionate portrait. Portrait can be depicted from different directions like front side portrait, side profile portrait, three quarter portraits etc., but for learning how to draw a portrait the practitioner must get to know the basic structure of a head. 1. Observe the basic shape of a head looks like a ball that needs to be flattened on the sides for making a front view of a head. 2. The head is not flat. It is three dimensional, like the ball given in the image. Observe the shape of skull and basic form of head. The large ball like circle is for cranial mass and the parts like nose, lips and chin are outside this circle. (Observe the image to understand the division and structure from the side view.)

Q: Portrait Practice #2: Explain the basic proportions of the front view portrait.

The image shows the division of the head, half horizontally and half vertically. The lines are the top and bottom points of head. The eyes are just on the central horizontal line. Now the half division of the bottom portion (chin to eyes) shows where end of the nose will be. Once more see the half division of the area (bottom of the nose to chin) for ending point of lips. The hair line is one third down from the top of the head to eyes portion and eye brows will be on the line just above the ears. Eyes are centered between the vertical central line and side of the head. The labelled lines in the diagram are: Vertical centerline, Hairline, Brow line, Horizontal centerline, Nose, Bottom lip and Chin.

lessons.title: 2.2 Landscape Paintings: Basic Perspective
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Perspective is a system of creating the illusion of a three dimensional space and feeling of distance on a two-dimensional surface.
  • Linear perspective is a mechanical means of demonstrating the visual appearances of planes and volumes in space; closer objects appear larger, distant objects appear smaller.
  • Eye level (also known as horizon line) is the artist's viewpoint, used as a reference to judge the scale and distance of objects.
  • The vanishing point (VP) is a point on the horizon line where parallel lines appear to converge as they recede.
  • Aerial perspective is the effect of atmosphere: distant objects fade, lighter in tone, less detailed and cooler in colour; nearer objects appear vivid, detailed and warmer.
  • Landscape practices: Watercolor Landscape Practices #1 and #2, Pastel color Landscape Practice #3 and Mix Media Landscape Practice #4.

Q: What is perspective? Define the basic terms of perspective used in landscape painting.

Perspective is a system of creating the illusion of a three dimensional space and feeling of distance on a two-dimensional surface. Linear Perspective is a mechanical means of demonstrating the visual appearances of planes and volumes in space. Objects which are closer, appear larger, while more distant objects appear smaller. Eye Level is the artist's viewpoint which is a view on a level with the artist's eyes. Also known as horizon line, a point of reference to judge the scale and distance of objects in relation to us. Horizon is a line running through a composition that represents the artist's viewpoint or eye level. This is the line on which two receding lines meet at a vanishing point. Vanishing Point (VP) is a point on the horizon line where the parallel lines appear to converge as they recede, according to the linear perspective. Aerial Perspective is the effect of atmosphere on the appearance of an object as it is viewed from a distance. The distant objects appear to fade, lighter in tone, less detailed, and bluer or cooler in colour; while the objects nearer to the viewer appear vivid, detailed and warmer in colour. The landscape practices of this chapter are: Watercolor Landscape Practice #1 and #2, Pastel color Landscape Practice #3 and Mix Media Landscape Practice #4.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Poster making is an important and prominent part of graphic design; a poster can be digitally designed and printed, or created by drawing, painting and calligraphy.
  • A typical poster presents both pictorial and textual elements, but it may be either completely textual or wholly pictorial; it should be communicative, informative and attractive.

Q: What is a poster? What are the qualities of a typical poster?

A typical poster presents both pictorial and textual element but it may be either completely textual or wholly pictorial. It should be communicative, informative and attractive. Usually posters are used for many purposes. Graphic Design is the art or profession of using design elements such as typography and images to convey information or create an effect.

Students can create posters manually by hand practice utilizing their skills of paintings and drawing or they may perform this task using the computer software like Photoshop, CorelDraw or paintbrush. Photoshop is a graphics editor developed and published by Adobe Inc. Coral Draw (Corel Draw) is a vector graphics editor.

lessons.title: 4.1 Introduction: Types of Sculpture
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Sculpture is one of the oldest branches of Visual Arts; it is a three dimensional form of visual representation and is also called plastic art.
  • Free standing round sculpture can be made in clay, stone, metal, bronze, copper, glass wires, plaster or fiberglass; one must walk around it for a complete look.
  • Relief sculpture is produced from a flat surface and viewed entirely from the front; its three methods are bas-relief (slightly raised), sunken relief or intaglio (carved out) and high relief (prominently raised, more than two levels).
  • Modern sculpture making uses welding, joining, mixing, molding and casting; casting pours a liquid material into a mold, and a mold is the negative or hollow cavity around a sculpted piece, made of plaster or silicon.
  • In the making practices, students first create three dimensional basic forms (cube, cone, hexagonal form, sphere, cylinder, pyramid) in clay and paper; three dimensional means having length, width and height.

Q: What is sculpture? Describe the types of sculpture.

Sculpture is one of the oldest branches of Visual Arts. It is three dimensional form of a visual representation. It is also called plastic art. Usually the known sculptural forms are carvings in stone and wood (chiseling and removing of the material to make the visual); this is also called relief sculpture, the round sculpture (three-dimensional representation of visuals using clay, stone, wood, metal, paper and many other materials). Now a days, there is a complete freedom to choose the material and process of sculpture making and as a result there is a vast variety of sculpture making by welding, joining, mixing, molding and casting procedures. Commonly we can find sculpture in the following types: 1. Free standing round sculpture: it can be in any material like clay, stone, any metal, bronze, copper, glass' wires, plaster, fiberglass etc. For having a complete look of the type of sculpture one must walk around it. 2. Relief Sculpture: this type of sculpture is produced from a flat surface and can be viewed entirely from the front. Relief is a sculptural technique where the sculpted elements remain attached to a flat background and can be viewed from one side only. Making of relief sculpture is usually practiced through three kinds of methods: i) Bas-relief: in which the design is managed in slightly raised surface from a flat background. ii) Sunken relief: it is also known as intaglio relief. In this process the artists create designs by carving out the flat background surface; either the design appears in the carved-out area or the untouched area of the background. iii) High relief: in this category the design of figures are prominently and dramatically raised from the flat background and artists can show more than two levels of the raised designs. Chiseling means to cut or carve with a sharp edged tool called chisel. Casting is a process used in sculpting, involving pouring a liquid material, such as Molten metal, plastic, rubber, plaster or fibreglass into the mold. Molding: A mold is the negative or hollow cavity produced around a sculpted piece for use in creating multiples of that piece. It can be made of plaster or silicon.

Q: What will the students learn in the making of sculpture practices?

Initially the students will focus on creating three dimensional basic forms using the materials like clay and paper. They will learn how to make a simplified three dimensional compositions with basic shapes both in clay and paper. Students will observe three dimensional shapes in the image given in the book for such practices (cube, cone, hexagonal form, sphere, cylinder, pyramid and other basic forms). Three Dimensional means having length, width and height.

lessons.title: Indus Valley Seals
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A seal is a carved device, a form of relief sculpture with an embossed design, used to create an impression on surfaces like wax, clay or paper.
  • Indus Valley seals might have been used for trade as stamps, for communicating messages, or as an individual's signature; their shapes include square, rectangle, circle, oval, cylindrical and disk, and their sizes range from less than an inch to 1.25 inches.
  • Most seals are carved in steatite (soapstone), as it can be easily carved; after carving, the stone was covered with alkali and heated to create luster.
  • The seal design has two parts — text and image; the unicorn (one-horned ox) appears in most seals, and the text on the seals is not yet deciphered.

Q: What do you know about Indus Valley Seals?

Seal is a carved device, a form of relief sculpture which has embossed design, used to create impression on the surfaces like wax, clay or paper. Among the artifacts excavated in the Indus Valley, Seals are of great importance. They might have been used for trade purpose as stamps, for communicating messages, or as individual's signature. The seals were carved in square, rectangle, circle, oval, cylindrical and disk like shape. Their sizes were as small as less than an inch to 1.25 inches. It is because of their small size that they are well preserved till after centuries, as compared to the other crafts of Indus Valley. Steatite stone (soapstone), limestone and marble were used. Most of the seals found are carved in steatite as it can be easily carved. Metal tools were used to cut and carve the stone. After carving, the stone was covered with alkali and then heated to create luster. The design of the seal consists of two parts, one having the text and the other having the image. Some seals also have symbolic shapes like circles and dots, linear patterns, crisscross pattern or the Pipal leave. At the back of the seal is a hole which might have served the purpose of holding or wearing as a ring or pendant. The carved images consist of the naturalistic figures of animals and sometimes stylized human figure. The animals depicted include tiger, elephant, one horned Indian rhinoceros, hare, crocodile, antelope, Brahman bull, unicorn and composite animal forms. An ox with a single horn, known as unicorn, is the animal which appears in most of the seals. A square seal depicting a three headed animal, carved in gray-brown steatite, is discovered from Mohenjodaro. The text carved out on the upper side of the seals is not yet deciphered.

lessons.title: Fasting Buddha from Gandhara
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The Buddhist art of Gandhara reached its peak during the Kushan period; its two sculpture types are High Relief (round sculptures attached with the background) and Low Relief.
  • The Fasting Buddha, one of the finest examples of Gandhara art, is made in schist stone, measures 84 cm and is displayed in the Lahore Museum.
  • It shows Buddha during the fast in search of enlightenment, which he gained at the age of thirty five; his weakened body and prominent rib cage show the artist's realistic study of the human skeleton.
  • Buddha sits in yogi pose with hands in the lap in dhyana mudra; the halo is the symbol of glory, the ushnisha is a slight lump on the head and the urna is a mark between the eyebrows.

Q: Write a short note on Fasting Buddha from Gandhara?

The Buddhist art of Gandhara reached its peak during the Kushan period. Buddha is always depicted seated in some certain position of hands and legs, or standing in a static pose. Two types of sculptures were found in Gandhara Art: 1. High Relief (Round sculptures but attached with the background). 2. Low Relief. The sculptures were placed in the monasteries and stupas, and were meant to decorate the architecture or for the worship. The sculpture of fasting Buddha is one of the finest examples of Gandhara art. It is made in schist stone, measures 84cm, and displayed in the Lahore Museum. The sculpture shows Buddha during the fast and in search of enlightenment. And as a result of it, his body weakened, and his bones became very prominent, particularly the rib cage reveals beneath the thin flesh. Eventually he gained enlightenment when he was thirty five years of age. The human body has been treated in a realistic way by the sculptor, which shows the artist's study of the human skeleton. Buddha is sitting in yogi pose with his hands set in the lap in the style known as dhyana mudra. There is halo at the back of the head which is the symbol of glory, ushnisha - a slight lump on the head and urna - a mark between the eyebrows. The growth of beard on Buddha's face is a rare depiction and shows that he completely disregarded his body during the fast. His eyes recede into the dark sockets and ears are elongated. A cloth covers his legs, while another cloth hangs from around the back on the arms. The pedestal on which the Buddha seats is carved with low relief depicting the figures of worshippers.

  • Makli Hill near Thatta is one of the largest graveyards in the world, used as a burial site from the 14th to 18th century CE; about 120,000 figures, including kings, queens, scholars and holy men, are buried there.
  • The Samma dynasty ruled Sindh from 1333 to 1524 AD; the reign of Jam Nizamuddin (1461–1508) was the longest and most glorious period.
  • Chaukandi graveyard near Karachi houses sandstone graves with intricate carvings; the tombs are attributed to the Jokhio and Baloch tribes and were built between the 15th and 19th centuries AD.
  • Chaukhandi literally means four corners; its yellow sandstone was acquired from Jungshahi near Thatta, and the most impressive tombs are like Egyptian pyramid structures with extraordinary geometric designs.

Q: Write a short note on Makli Hill Tombs.

Makli hill near Thatta, Pakistan, is one of the largest graveyards in the world housing a magnificent collection of historic Middle Eastern tombs. From 14th to 18th century CE, the local royal families inhabiting in Thatta used Makli Hill as a comman burial site. "The Samma dynasty ruled over Sindh as an independent country for more than 190 years i.e. from 1333 to 1524 A.D. The reign of Jam Nizamuddin was not only the longest one (1461 - 1508), but is considered to be the most glorious period in the history of Sindh." All the successive rulers built and elaborated differing tomb structures, thus creating profusion of varied designs of graves. Figures of great importance, around some 120,000, were buried there, including kings, queens, scholars, holy men, and other significant figures. Apart from tombs, there are also found mosques, temples, swimming pools, educational institutions, manuscripts, recreation halls. "Jam Nizamuddin Sammo (Sultan Nizamuddin Shah) like other Samma rulers is also buried in Makli historical graveyard near Thatta. His tomb is an exemplary pattern of architecture. A row of birds, sun flowers, lotus arrangement on its walls as well as windows (Jharoka) show that Sindh has its glorious past even in the primitive ages." The tombs constructed in stone are categorized into four different periods of creation according to the ruling body at the time. Some of the tombs comprise of tall columns, whereas others are ornamented with arches. Altogether, the hill is an assemblage of varied architectural motifs. Some of the graves are inscribed with Quranic verses, while some structures show Hindu architectural elements.

Q: Write a short note on Chaukandi Tombs.

Chaukandi graveyard is another example of exquisitely constructed tombs. It is located near Karachi and houses sandstone graves embellished with stone carvings consisting of intricate patterns, and are remarkably well-preserved. "Chaukhandi Tombs are generally attributed to the Jokhio and Baloach Tribes of Sindh and were built between the fifteenth and nineteenth centuries A.D. Chaukhandi literally means four corners. The tombs are built of yellow sand stone which were acquired from Jungshahi, a railway station near Thatta." "The most impressive tombs are like Egyptian pyramid structures. They are rectangular in shape... The geometric designs that cover the entire surface of the tombs are extra ordinary. The intricate carving in geometric designs is unique and its delicacy gives the impression of wood carving. It is interesting to mention that the same designs are found in the textile pattern, jewellery and wood carving in Sindh and Balochistan today... These tombs found only in Sindh and Balochistan can be seen along the Makran coast by the Indus river upto Sehwan Sharif. The most elaborately carved tombs are located at sites such as Haidan, Lasbella and other places."

lessons.title: Shahid Sajjad and Rabia Zuberi
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Shahid Sajjad (1937–2014), an internationally celebrated sculptor of Pakistan, began with large wooden figurative sculptures inspired by the villages of East Bengal; after training with a Japanese master he cast small bronze sculptures of organic forms based on human figures.
  • He won the first prize at the National Sculpture Exhibition, Islamabad in 1977, and executed the bronze mural 'Cavalry through the Ages' for the Pakistan Army in 1981.
  • Rabia Zuberi, one of Pakistan's pioneer women sculptors (born 1940), established Karachi's first art school, the Karachi School of Art, in 1964.
  • Her masterpiece 'Peace Message to the Progressive World' — seven figures, each seven feet tall, in a circular composition ten feet in diameter, in bronze, fiber and steel — is part of the national collection at the National Art Gallery, Islamabad; the recurring theme of her work is humanism.

Q: Write a note about Shahid Sajjad a prominent sculptor of Pakistan?

Shahid Sajjad (1937-2014) is one of the prominent and internationally celebrated sculptors of Pakistan. "At a young age, he became interested in calligraphy and soon mastered the skill. He practiced drawing and carefully observed signboard painters at work. He became a successful commercial artist, dabbling in film making and painting. A restless soul, he spent three years travailing across Europe and Asia on a motorcycle. He was particularly fascinated by the woodcarving of Bali, the Philippines and Japan, and by wood reliefs by Paul Gauguin in the Musée du Louvre, Paris, France." Shahid Sajjad, started his professional career as a sculptor with large wooden figurative sculptures. In these works his source of inspiration was the sophisticated beauty of the East Bengal villages. After a training with a Japanese master, his work developed to the phase when he began casting small bronze sculptures having "organic forms based on human figures." In the late 1990s he returned to wood, making figures of male and mother and child carved out of single piece. The sculptures of mother and child have interlocked parts and are well expressive of the meaning. He used to prepare the wood for carving from the fallen trees, and while this process he learnt about textures and characteristics of different kind of woods. In 1974, his solo exhibition of wood and bronze sculptures was held at the Karachi Arts Council. In 1977, at the National Sculptures Exhibition which was held in Islamabad, he won the first prize. He executed a commissioned mural in bronze for the Pakistan Army entitled Cavalry through the Ages in 1981. His next mural in cold cast bronze was for the Maritime Museum in Karachi. An exhibition held in 1994 displayed a collection of large sculptures having carved forms titled as My Primitives which depicted his visit to the Rangamati forest in Bangladesh. In 1996, he became a fellow at National College of Arts. He was also one of the founding member of Indus Valley School of Art and Architecture in Karachi.

Q: What do you know about the sculptures done by Rabia Zuberi?

Rabia Zuberi is one of the Pakistan's pioneer woman sculptors. She born in India in 1940 and devoted her life to flourish the art and art education in Pakistan. She graduated from Aligarh University India in 1959. Later she got enrolled in Govt. Art College Lucknow India for a graduate degree in sculpture. Rabia Zuberi remained enthusiastically engaged to promote the art education and establishment of new art institute and galleries in Pakistan along her sister Hajra Mansoor and later joined by Mansur Rahi a well known artist of Pakistan. She established Karachi's first art school, Karachi School of Art (KSA) in 1964. This institute acclaimed the production of numerous fine artists and educationists. Her masterpiece: an artwork consisting of seven figures, each one seven feet tall in a circular composition ten feet in diameter is titled: Peace Message to the Progressive World. It is the culmination of three years of intensive work in the media of bronze fiber and steel, and is part of the national collection shown at the National Art Gallery, Islamabad. She is also a fine painter and her drawings often carry an architectural linearity. The recurring theme of Zuberi's artworks is humanism. Through the medium of drawing, painting and sculpture, she voices out to the world to seek for love, forgiveness, social justice and peace. She is the recipient of numerous national awards for art including the President's Pride of Performance and the Lifetime Achievement Award.

lessons.title: Pottery and Ceramics of Mehrgarh
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Mehrgarh, on the Kacchi Plain of Balochistan, is the oldest and most important Neolithic site (6500 BCE to 2500 BCE) of the Indus Valley civilization, from where the oldest ceramic figurines of South Asia were found.
  • Evidence of the potter's wheel was found at Mehrgarh; its pottery carries animal motifs and intricate designs, the most common motifs being Pipal leaf, fish and geometric patterns.
  • Painted pottery, detailed terracotta figures, glazed beads and the first terracotta seals belong to this period; pottery prepared on the potter's wheel and red ware terracotta pottery are hallmarks of Mehrgarh.
  • The female figurines of Mehrgarh, painted and decorated with ornaments and varied hairstyles, are considered to be mother goddesses.

Q: What do you know about the pottery and ceramics found in Mehrgarh?

Mehrgarh is the oldest and most important Neolithic (6500 BCE to 2500 BCE) sites of the Indus Valley civilization. It is located on the Kacchi Plain of Balochistan, Pakistan. "Many artifacts as human figurines, pottery and copper items found there show the culture and tradition of the people lived there. Moreover, Mehrgarh is the city, from where the oldest ceramic figurines of South Asia were found." With the discovery of the evidence of potter's wheel in Mehrgarh the archeologists found pottery items in abundance. These pots have animal motifs along intricate designs. Female figurines are elaborated with sophisticated designs. The most common motifs which appear on different pottery are Pipal leaf, fish and geometric patterens. However, with passage of time the quality and intricacy of designs seem to have suffered due to mass production and due to a growing interest in bronze and copper vessels at those times. "In Mehrgarh, ceramic technology had been discovered and largely used. Fine specimens of painted pottery have been excavated, along with detailed terracotta figures and glazed beads. The first terracotta seals also belong to this period." Pottery prepared on potter's wheel and red ware terracotta potteries are hallmarks of Mehrgarh. Apart from the fish motif and pipal leaf pattern this pottery is characterized by rosettes, butterfly patterns, chequer board pattern, geometric designs of dot tip motifs, hatched or plain triangles. Terracotta figures of women and animals have also been found along with glazed pottery and glazed faience beads. Female figurines were painted and decorated with ornaments and varied hairstyles. These female figurines are considered to be mother goddesses.

lessons.title: Pottery of Harappa and Mohenjodaro
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In most houses of Harappa and Mohenjodaro there was a potter's wheel; by material, the pottery is categorized into stone vases and earthenware vases, the earthenware being the characteristic artifact of the Indus Valley.
  • Pottery was used for two main purposes: utilitarian (storing food, grains, oil and crops) and funerary and ritual purposes; it was also exported for trade.
  • The pots were shaped on the potter's wheel or free hand, baked in kilns (round with domed tops, or fire-pits) and polished with a bone or stone; the Indus people were skilled in baking and had knowledge of controlled firing.
  • Colour schemes used for decoration are buff or pink, red and black, and white and green; the motifs are floral, geometric and figural.

Q: Write a short note on the pottery found in Indus Valley sites of Harappa and Mohenjodaro.

A variety of pottery has been found in Harappa and Mohenjodaro. In most of the houses there was a potter's wheel. The vessels are of different sizes and shapes according to their use in the daily life. According to the material used in the making, the pottery can be categorized in two groups, i.e. stone vases and earthenware vases. The unavailability of stone in the Indus Valley region suggests that it was imported from other regions. Stone pottery was used to grind something or as oil jars. While the earthenware vases are the characteristic artifact of the Indus Valley. The fertile clay form the nearby river was used for the pottery which is found in numerous styles, types, shapes and design. There were two main purposes for which the pottery was used; number one the utilitarian purpose, and number two funerary and ritual purposes. The utilitarian pottery was used to store food, grains, oil and even crops; whereas a great number of funeral pottery has been excavated from the graves which were buried with the dead. Moreover, the pottery was also exported to other regions for the trade purpose. The pottery consists of shapes and styles: goblets (small glasses), shallow dishes (plates), bowls and cups for domestic use, beaker type jar, jar with pedestal, ledge necked jar, vase like pots, heavy based jars with lids, ribbed pottery, storage jars, perforated jars as strainers, kidney shaped designs, miniature vessels to keep perfume, tiny pots with narrow opening to contain eye powder, small trays for liquids, large jars buried in the earth to keep family treasure, jars with narrow neck and elongated shape, small dishes and pots for religious offerings and jars with round or pointed base. The pottery is ornamented with decorative motifs consisting of floral motifs, geometric motifs and figural motifs. The color schemes used for the decoration of pottery are: 1. Buff or pink. 2. Red and black. 3. White and green. "The pottery of Indus Valley civilization is an excellent example of ancient glazed pottery." The pots were shaped on the potter's wheel and sometimes made free hand, after which they were baked in kiln. After painting and decorating, the pot was polished with a bone or stone. The kilns were round with domed tops, while some were in the form of fire-pit. Indus valley people were skilled in baking and had knowledge of controlled firing.

lessons.title: Mian Salahuddin and Masood Kohari
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Mian Salahuddin (1938–2006), among the few ceramicists of Pakistan, graduated from the National College of Arts and studied ceramics under the Japanese ceramist Koichi Takita Sensei; his ceramic pieces modify traditional pottery into sculptures.
  • He used ashes of burnt leaves and branches in his glazes, which change the colours to earth tones; after molding and drying, the clay pieces are baked, sanded and then glazed.
  • Masood Kohari (1939–present), one of Pakistan's finest ceramic artists, began his ceramics with a visit to Thatta; the trip to Hala, the traditional center of Sindhi pottery, decided him to work seriously in the medium.
  • In 1964 Kohari worked with the ceramic craftsmen of Gujranwala; his 1968 Karachi Arts Council show included four 8-feet tall columns, 70 wall based reliefs and the tile series 'War and Peace'. He has lived in Paris since 1969 and says: 'I am not potter, I am painter in clay.'

Q: What do you know about the ceramic art of Mian Salahuddin?

Mian Salahuddin (1938-2006) was among a few ceramicists in Pakistan. He graduated from the National College of Arts and studied ceramics under Japanese ceramist, Koichi Takita Sensei. He had later been linked with NCA as a Ceramics teacher. His works consists of diverse variety of mediums including paper, wood, glass, steel and primarily clay. His ceramic pieces depict the modification of traditional pottery into sculptures representing certain meanings. Among the sources of inspiration for his works, the most important are the words which he wanted to express. Moreover, he took the natural forms which he manipulated in his art work. His subsequent works lack details and are more symbolic. He was of the view that the medium used by the artist influences his personality, so did the clay influence his temperament. "I do not think of an audience, I simply work to please myself. I do not care about who is going to buy it, or like it, or even look at it." After molding and drying, the clay pieces are baked, sanded and then glazed. Mian Salahuddin said, "When leaves are falling from the trees I collect my materials; leaves and branches, which when burnt leave behind ashes that are used in the glaze. These ashes change the colors to earth tones. I love the colors of the earth, not raw but subtle, mellow tones. Ceramics as an art is unappreciated. There are problems with materials, few outlets and the public generally do not understand non-utility pottery. That is why so few artists and sculptors go into this field. For me it is a labor of love." He was profoundly experimental with different methods, techniques and media. By re-cycling the nature through the ashes of the fallen leaves, Mian Salahuddin referred to immortality and also the nature-cycle. The forms created by his hands reflect his inner emotions. Most of his artworks are based on ironic ideas. The glazes depict his richness of imagination. Each ceramic piece is a work of visual pleasure consisting of connected parts unparalleled in the art world. "Wall based horses and rams heads, conical paper weights, and a diverse array of forms" all reveal his conceptual approach.

Q: Write a note on Masood Kohari's work in ceramics?

Masood Kohari (1939-Present): Masood Kohari's work is mostly in ceramics and he is one of Pakistan's finest ceramic artists. Also, his drawings, paintings and crystal collages are world famous. His endeavors in ceramics started with his visit to Thatta. "For centuries ceramics have been considered medium of artistic expression in Thatta... The artist in Kohari was deeply fascinated by this medium. Inspired, he made exploratory trip to Hala, another town in Sind, which is traditionally the center of Sindhi pottery. The trip to Hala decided Kohari to work seriously in the new medium." He took some material from potters and designed some tiles in blue and white illustrating his typical figural style. "In 1964 when he went off to Gujranwala... formed strong ties working with the ceramic craftsmen, learning about clay and beginning a life-long fascination with the qualities of clay and fire." "To learn the age-old secrets of shaping, firing and glazing wet clay into toys, jars and vases, he decided to live with these craftsmen, whose trade had been handed down from father to son, for centuries." He became a master in firing and glazing techniques. He experimented by deliberately ignoring the conventional use of oxides and by letting them take unusual patterns. He was used to shape his vases, bowls and jars in distorted non-functional forms, and sometimes even with cracks due to over firing. He carved the life of the craftsmen of Gujranwala on the tiles and pottery depicting the farmers, cows, houses, children and womenfolk. In 1968, he... mounted a spectacular ceramics show at the Karachi Arts Council. It included four brilliantly colored, 8ft tall columns measuring 15 inches in circumference; 70 wall based reliefs, large urns, and a series of tiles he titled: War and Peace. "Kohari's desire to work with glass led him to France where he visited established glass studios and workshops, and on to the famous glass artworks center of Marino near Venice in Italy." He has been living in Paris since 1969, has been practicing crystal fire paintings and crystal collages. He exhibits in Parisian galleries and Pakistani as well. He claims, "I am not potter, I am painter in clay".

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Textiles, pottery, metal ware and wood work are the well-known utilitarian crafts of Pakistan; the craftsmen have been the vital link for communication and exchange of cultures between civilizations.
  • Bronze and copper finds from Mohenjodaro and Taxila link the current crafts to the 5000 years old Indus Valley and Gandhara civilizations; specialists working on knives and daggers are found in Wazirabad.
  • Metal craft includes casting, cutting, engraving, piercing, enameling and Koftgari; high quality silver work is produced in Kashmir and Peshawar is specially noted for its cutwork metal ware.
  • Koftgari, the art of inlaying or encrusting gold and silver wire on baser metal, was originally introduced by the Mughals; its main centers are Lahore, Gujrat and Sialkot, and it is specially applied on hookahs and jewellery boxes.

Q: What do you know about metal craft of Pakistan?

The people of Pakistan can take pride in the rich and varied cultural tradition of art and craft. Textiles, pottery, metal ware and wood woks are considered among its well-known utilitarian crafts of the country. Tracing the source of creative intellect, it was found that the craftsmen managed to develop an unbroken chain of traditional art and craft since the centuries on this region. The craftsmen had been the vital link for communication and exchange of cultures between civilizations. Civilizations have come and gone, but the craftsmen have survived. To somehow the genius of the craftsmen from Sindhi, Baluchi, Kashmiri, Punjabi or Pakhtoon found the richest expression of cultural traditions in continuity which remained intact since ages. "The metals, brass and copper, have been in use in this country since time immemorial. Recovery of bronze and copper utensils, figurines and coins from the excavations of Mohenjodaro and Taxila link the current crafts of the country to the 5000 years old Indus valley and the Gandhara civilizations. Beauty and skillful workmanship in metal ware is also found in areas of Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhawa. Specialists working on knives and daggers are found in Wazirabad. Artisans working in this medium use intricate filigree and chasing for their products in other regions, such as Sindh also." Metal craft includes casting, cutting, engraving, piercing, enameling and Koftgari. High quality in silver works is produced in Kashmir. Brass and copper ware are made in Lahore, Karachi, Multan and a number of cities but Peshawar is specially noted for its cutwork metal ware. "Koftgari or the art of inlaying or encrusting gold and silver wire on baser metal was originally introduced by the Mughals. Lahore, Gujrat and Sialkot are its main centers. This is specially applied on hookas and jewellery boxes. Enameling or enamel inlaying is done in Kashmir and parts of Punjab, Karachi, Hyderabad, Multan and Lahore."

lessons.title: Indus Dancing Girl
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The Indus Dancing Girl is a tiny bronze-cast statue of a young lady, dating to about 2500 BC, recovered in excavation from Mohenjo-daro; it is one of the rarest artifacts in the world.
  • It shows that the Indus artists knew metal blending and casting, and that the society had developed dance and other performing arts as modes of entertainment.
  • Her left arm is covered entirely with heavy ringed bangles, while her right arm has just two heavy rings; she wears a necklace with four 'phalis' like shaped pendants.
  • The sculpture is now in the collection of the National Museum, New Delhi, India.

Q: Write a short note on Indus Dancing Girl?

This ancient sculpture is one of the rarest artifacts in the world. It is a unique blend of antiqueness, art, lifestyle, taste and cultural excellence of a people in such remote past as about 2500 BC. It is a tiny bronze-cast which represents the statue of a young lady commonly known as 'Indus dancing girl'. This female figure sculpture is stylistically posed and performing a dance. The forward thrust of the left leg and backwards tilted right, the gesture of the hands, demeanor of the face and uplifted head, all speak of absorption in dance, perhaps one of those early styles that combined drama with dance, and dialogue with body-gestures. As was not unusual in the lifestyle of early days, the young lady has been cast as nude. The statue, recovered in excavation from an area of Mohenjo-daro, is suggestive of two major breaks-through, one, that the Indus artists knew metal blending and casting and perhaps other technical aspects of metallurgy, and two, that a well developed society Indus people had innovated dance and other performing arts as modes of entertainment. Large eyes, flat nose, well-fed cheeks, bunched curly hair and broad forehead define the iconography of the lady, while a tall figure with large legs and arms, high neck, subdued belly, her anatomy is carefully rendered. The adornment of her left arm is widely different from the right. While just two, though heavy, rings adorn her right arm, the left is covered in entirety with heavy ringed bangles. Besides, the figure has been cast as wearing a necklace with four 'phalis' like shaped pendants. Though a small work of art, it is impressive and surpasses in plasticity and heavily ornate terracotta figurines of Indus valley excavations. (The sculpture is now in the collection of National Museum New Delhi India.)

lessons.title: Coins and Armor in South Asia
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Coins are one of the basic sources of history; the Numismatic Department of the National Museum of Pakistan possesses about ninety thousand ancient coins.
  • Coinage in South Asia is traced back to about the 6th century BC; Shershah Suri introduced the silver rupee and copper coin, the British introduced standard coins in 1818, and a pure nickel rupee was introduced in 1946.
  • Minting or coining is the process of manufacturing coins using a kind of stamping; it is classified into hammered coinage and milled coinage.
  • Mughal era armor — Kulah Khud (helmets), Zirrah Baktar (protective jackets), Talwar (sword) and Dhaal (shield) — was elaborately decorated with filigree, Koftgari and Quranic calligraphy; the Mughals excelled in chain mail and scale mail, the most powerful armors of that time.

Q: Write a short essay on the history of coins in South Asia?

Among the other relics of the past, coins occupy an eminent place. These are of the basic sources of history. They are reflected the political, social and cultural activities of a nation. The Numismatic Department of the National Museum of Pakistan possesses about the Ninety thousand of ancient Coins in its collection belonging to different periods. The history of coinage is traced back to about 6th century B.C. in the region of South Asia. In the ancient times metals like gold, silver, iron, pots and axes were used as a medium of exchange in the old India. History tells that guptas, King Altamash and Mohammad Bin Tughlaq tried their best to introduce coins in the country. Shershah Suri introduced the silver rupee and copper coin. Akbar and Aurangzeb also contributed in this process. After the fall of Mughal Empire the state was divided into small states. Every state has its own coins. There were more than 1000 different coins of various types in the subcontinent when English came in the India. They introduced the standard coins in 1818. The coinage of gold standard remained continued. The British Government demonetized silver rupee in 1941 and 1943. A pure nickel rupee was introduced in 1946. Later on the independence reserve bank of India issued the coins till June 30, 1948, which were used as legal tender money up to one year. Making of Coins: "In minting, coining or coinage is the process of manufacturing coins using a kind of stamping which is now generically known in metalworking as "coining". This process is different from cast coinage, and can be classified in hammered coinage or hammering and milled coinage or milling." The coin-making process takes hundreds of hours of careful work to get from the initial idea to the finished coin: 1. The proposed design of the coin is sent to the relevant Minister for approval before proceeding to the next stage. 5. One of the Mint's robots tips the blanks into a hopper and they travel along a conveyor belt to the coin presses. 6. The design is 'pressed' into the reverse (tails) of the blank at the same time as the portrait or the front design is pressed into the obverse (head) of the coin. 7. Finished coins are packed and sent to banks around the country.

Q: What do you know about the usage and appearance of armor in South Asia?

In modern days the concept of armor, artillery or military weapons is drastically changed than its usage and appearance in the past. Armors and weapons or war equipments have grown more powerful, shorter and simplified with every passing year. To prevent the most powerful bullets Kevlar jackets or vests are using. "Kevlar vests of the 1970s still form the basis of most modern body armor" which do not have any lavish appearance while the armor from the recent past of South Asian region, from the Mughal dynasty and the time right after the Mughals demonstrate a history of artillery as an art of war equipments with more elaborated, ornamented and artistic manifestation. Thus such examples of armors or artillery became the most interesting part of modern day art history and museums. "During its peak the Mughal dynasty (1526-1857) flourished as a result of a strong centralized government, an increase in trade, and the rise of new markets in urban centers such as Delhi, Agra, Lahore, Dhaka, Surat, and Masulipatnam. Indo-Islamic architecture reached its apogee under the empire, with opulent palaces, tombs, forts, mosques, and gardens. The Mughals ruled the area of present-day Afghanistan, Pakistan, and much of northern India. The years of Mughal preeminence saw extraordinary developments in artillery civil and war administration." Kulah Khud (helmets), Zirrah Baktar (protective jackets), Talwar (sword), Dhaal (protective shield), horse and elephants protective covers, daggers and many other things of artillery were heavily elaborated and decorated with the techniques like filigree, Koftgari, patterned motifs of inlaid brass, silver or gold; or decorated with figurative images or even with the calligraphic inscriptions from Holy Quran, hypothetically to gain "Help from Allah and a speedy victory. Mughals were excelled in the techniques of 'Chain mail' and 'Scale mail. Both techniques developed the most powerful armors of that time.

Q: The craftsmen had been the vital link for ______________ between civilizations.

(a) Wars and unrest (b) communication and exchange of cultures (c) cultural envy (d) entertainment
Correct answer: communication and exchange of cultures

Q: Recovery of bronze and copper utensils, figurines and coins from the excavations of Mohenjodaro and Taxila link the current crafts of the country to the 5000 years old ______________.

(a) Soan Vallery (b) Indus Valley (c) Nile Valley (d) Neelum Valley
Correct answer: Indus Valley

Q: Skillful workmanship in metal ware is also found in areas of Punjab and ______________.

(a) Harappa (b) Mohenjo-Daro (c) Mehrgarh (d) Afghanistan
Correct answer: Mohenjo-Daro

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Glossary terms A to E, as defined in the book: from Aerial Perspective, Alabaster and Anatomy to Draftsmanship, Drip-stone and Earthenware.
  • Key terms in this part: Casting (pouring a liquid material into the mold), Chiseling (to cut or carve with a chisel) and Dhyana Mudra (the gesture of meditation).

Q: What is meant by 'Aerial Perspective'?

The effect of atmosphere on the appearance of an object as it is viewed from a distance. The distant objects appear to fade, lighter in tone, less detailed, and bluer or cooler in colour; while the objects nearer to the viewer appear vivid, detailed and warmer in colour.

Q: What is meant by 'Alabaster'?

A finely granular variety of gypsum, often white and translucent, used for sculptures.

Q: What is meant by 'Alkali'?

A base, having pH greater than 7.0, that dissolves in water.

Q: What is meant by 'Amulet'?

An object, either natural or man-made, believed to be endowed with special powers to protect or bring good fortune.

Q: What is meant by 'Anatomy'?

A study of the structure or internal workings of something, like human body, animal or plant.

Q: What is meant by 'Arabesque'?

A form of surface decorations based on rhythmic linear patterns of scrolling and interlacing foliage, tendrils or plain lines, often combined with other Elements.

Q: What is meant by 'Archeology'?

Study of the material remains of past human life, activities and artifacts.

Q: What is meant by 'Artifact'?

A handmade object, characteristic of an earlier time or cultural stage, especially an object found at an archaeological excavation.

Q: What is meant by 'Artillery'?

Heavy military ranged weapons.

Q: What is meant by 'Book Illustration'?

A form of fine art that is used to create drawn pictures and images for books to help add to or enhance the story for better understanding.

Q: What is meant by 'Burin needle'?

A tool used for engraving or carving.

Q: What is meant by 'Casting'?

A process used in sculpting, involving pouring a liquid material, such as Molten metal, plastic, rubber, plaster or fibreglass into the mold.

Q: What is meant by 'Canopy'?

An architectural structure with an overhead roof structure that has open sides.

Q: What is meant by 'Ceramics'?

Heat-resistant object made out of clay and permanently hardened by heat.

Q: What is meant by 'Chevron line'?

Zigzag line.

Q: What is meant by 'Chiseling'?

To cut or carve with a sharp edged tool called chisel.

Q: What is meant by 'Craft'?

A creative object consisting of manual skill.

Q: What is meant by 'Column'?

In architecture, a column is an upright pillar or post, which supports a roof or a beam.

Q: What is meant by 'Composition'?

A balanced arrangement of visual elements in an artwork using various principles and Techniques.

Q: What is meant by 'Conceptual art'?

Art which focuses on ideas and purposes.

Q: What is meant by 'Contemporary'?

Belonging to the present time and current situations.

Q: What is meant by 'Contour'?

A contour line defines the outline of a form, as well as interior structure, without the use of shading.

Q: What is meant by 'Contrast'?

A large difference between two things to create interest in an artwork. Contrast can be between the tones, or between the textures, etc.

Q: What is meant by 'Convention'?

An established norm or trend within a particular society or region.

Q: What is meant by 'Coral Draw'?

A vector graphics editor.

Q: What is meant by 'Corrugated sheet'?

A thick paper having fluted texture.

Q: What is meant by 'Dhyana Mudra'?

Means gesture of meditation. It is Buddha's figure in posture of contemplation, with closed eyes, and hands resting on the lap with palms (facing upwards) laid one over the other.

Q: What is meant by 'Draftsmanship'?

Quality skill of drawing.

Q: What is meant by 'Drip-stone'?

Moulding over a door or window which deflects Rain.

Q: What is meant by 'Earthenware'?

Glazed or unglazed terracotta pottery.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Glossary terms E to P, as defined in the book: from Expression, Eye Level and Faience to Photoshop, Pictorial, Plastic art and Portrait.
  • Key terms in this part: Koftgari (work in which metal is inlaid with gold or silver), Molding (the negative or hollow cavity around a sculpted piece) and Perspective (creating the illusion of three dimensional space on a two-dimensional surface).

Q: What is meant by 'Expression'?

Conveying or indicating one's feelings and emotions through any medium like painting, sculpture, poetry, etc.

Q: What is meant by 'Eye Level'?

Artist's viewpoint which is a view on a level with the artist's eyes. Also known as horizon line, a point of reference to judge the scale and distance of objects in relation to us.

Q: What is meant by 'Faience'?

Finely glazed ceramic beads, figures and other small objects.

Q: What is meant by 'Filigree'?

Intricate metalwork.

Q: What is meant by 'Fixative'?

A liquid, similar to varnish, which is usually sprayed over a finished piece of artwork, usually a dry media artwork, to better preserve it and prevent smudging.

Q: What is meant by 'Form'?

Objects that are either three dimensional or appear to be three dimensional.

Q: What is meant by 'Graphic Design'?

Art or profession of using design elements such as typography and images to convey information or create an effect.

Q: What is meant by 'Graphite'?

A form of carbon which leaves a shiny metallic gray color on a surface when moved across it. It can be removed with an eraser. The most common form of graphite is the "lead" inside a pencil, compressed and baked to varying degrees of hardness.

Q: What is meant by 'Gum-Arabic'?

A natural gum used as binding agent for water based paints.

Q: What is meant by 'Halo'?

A round or elliptical disk behind or over the head of holy or important figures.

Q: What is meant by 'Horizon'?

A line running through a composition that represents the artist's viewpoint or eye level. This is the line on which two receding lines meet at a vanishing point.

Q: What is meant by 'Illustration'?

A visual explanation of a text, concept or process.

Q: What is meant by 'Jali'?

A form of architectural decoration consisting of perforated stone or latticed screen, usually ornamented with constructed geometrical pattern.

Q: What is meant by 'Kiln'?

An oven, furnace, or heated enclosure used for processing a substance (like clay) by burning or firing.

Q: What is meant by 'Koftgari'?

Work in which metal is inlaid with gold or silver.

Q: What is meant by 'Life Drawing'?

A drawing of the human form in any of its various postures using any of the drawing media.

Q: What is meant by 'Linear Perspective'?

A mechanical means of demonstrating the visual appearances of planes and volumes in space. Objects which are closer, appear larger, while more distant objects appear smaller.

Q: What is meant by 'Luster'?

Shine created by the glaze or reflecting light.

Q: What is meant by 'Metallurgy'?

Technique or science of working or heating metals so as to give them certain desired shapes or properties.

Q: What is meant by 'Molding'?

A mold is the negative or hollow cavity produced around a sculpted piece for use in creating multiples of that piece. It can be made of plaster or silicon.

Q: What is meant by 'Mudra'?

Symbolic body and hand gestures in Buddhism.

Q: What is meant by 'Mural'?

Any piece of artwork painted or applied directly on a wall, ceiling or other permanent surfaces.

Q: What is meant by 'Naturalistic'?

A true-to-life style representation in art which depicts close representation of nature.

Q: What is meant by 'Paper mache'?

Paper pulp mixed with glue, pressed together, and molded when moist to form various objects, which becomes hard and strong when dry.

Q: What is meant by 'Parapet'?

A low protective wall or barrier at the edge of a balcony, roof, bridge, or the like.

Q: What is meant by 'Perspective'?

A system of creating the illusion of a three dimensional space and feeling of distance on a two-dimensional surface.

Q: What is meant by 'Photoshop'?

A graphics editor developed and published by Adobe Inc.

Q: What is meant by 'Pictorial'?

Consisting of pictures.

Q: What is meant by 'Plastic art'?

Works of art in which materials and elements capable of being molded, modified or transformed are used, e.g. ceramics or sculpture.

Q: What is meant by 'Portrait'?

A painting, photograph, sculpture, or other artistic representation of a person, in which the face and its expression is depicted.

lessons.title: Glossary (P to V)
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Glossary terms P to V, as defined in the book: from Pottery, Profile and Proportion to Urna, Ushnisha, Value and Vanishing Point.
  • Key terms in this part: Relief (sculpted elements attached to a flat background), Shade (a colour mixed with black), Tint (a colour mixed with white) and Tone (a colour mixed with gray).

Q: What is meant by 'Pottery'?

The process and the products of forming vessels, pots, dishes, and other articles with clay and then fired. Pottery can be broadly divided into earthenware, porcelain, and stoneware.

Q: What is meant by 'Profile'?

View Side view of a portrait.

Q: What is meant by 'Proportion'?

The comparative relationship of one object to another with respect to size, quantity, or degree.

Q: What is meant by 'Realism / Realistic'?

The arts that attempts to represent subject matter truthfully, without artificiality.

Q: What is meant by 'Relief'?

Sculptural technique where the sculpted elements remain attached to a flat background and can be viewed from one side only.

Q: What is meant by 'Seal'?

A stamping device with carved imagery, for making an impression in wax, clay, paper, or some other medium, including an embossment on paper.

Q: What is meant by 'Shading'?

A range of darkness by applying media more densely or with a darker shade for darker areas, and less densely or with a lighter shade for lighter areas.

Q: What is meant by 'Shade'?

The mixture of a colour with black, which reduces lightness.

Q: What is meant by 'Shape'?

An enclosed area defined on a two dimensional Surface.

Q: What is meant by 'Silhouette'?

A two-dimensional representation of the outline of an object, uniformly filled in with colour.

Q: What is meant by 'Steatite'?

A type of stone used for sculpture carving.

Q: What is meant by 'Stoneware'?

Glazed or unglazed white clay pottery.

Q: What is meant by 'Stylized'?

Depiction or treatment of image in a non realistic style.

Q: What is meant by 'Superimposed'?

Something placed or laid over or above something.

Q: What is meant by 'Symbol'?

Something used for representing an abstract idea.

Q: What is meant by 'Symmetrical'?

An object or composition is symmetrical when its one side mirrors its other side.

Q: What is meant by 'Textual'?

Relating to a text.

Q: What is meant by 'Texture'?

The surface quality or feel of an object, its smoothness, roughness, softness, etc.

Q: What is meant by 'Terracotta'?

Baked red clay.

Q: What is meant by 'Three Dimensional'?

Having length, width and height.

Q: What is meant by 'Tint'?

The mixture of a color with white, which increases lightness.

Q: What is meant by 'Tone'?

Tone of a colour is produced by the mixture of that colour with gray.

Q: What is meant by 'Torso'?

The trunk of a human body-excluding arms, legs, and head.

Q: What is meant by 'Trefoil pattern'?

Three petaled flower pattern.

Q: What is meant by 'Tradition'?

Beliefs or customs passed down within a group, society or a region, with symbolic meaning or special significance with origins in the past.

Q: What is meant by 'Two dimensional'?

Flat surface, having only length and width.

Q: What is meant by 'Urna'?

A mark between the eye brows of Buddha, representing the third eye.

Q: What is meant by 'Ushnisha'?

Hair bun on the top of the head of Buddha.

Q: What is meant by 'Value'?

The lightness or darkness of a color.

Q: What is meant by 'Vanishing Point (VP)'?

A point on the horizon line where the parallel lines appear to converge as they recede, according to the linear perspective.
